product: US corn & soybean — in-season area forecast
headline_basis: area of the published 5 m classification (pixel count)
usda_note: USDA comparison = model acres vs June Acreage planted acres, summed over states whose classified cells cover at least 97% of Census land area; partly covered states are listed but not compared. June Acreage is a survey estimate, not a measurement: it is revised in later reports and is published without an error term here, so a difference is a disagreement between two estimates rather than our error alone.
admin_note: County and state figures are the counted area of the published 5 m map of classified fields -- one direct pixel count, deduplicated across overlapping MGRS tiles, then binned for the roll-up. The 95% interval is classification error from the error matrix at this lead time, not sampling error. Counties sum to their state; states sum to the belt.
pixel_note: The published 5 m map of classified corn and soybean fields, drawn as polygons so it stays sharp at any zoom. These are the pixels the acreage is counted from, with one exception: the layer draws the full classified extent, including the Canadian ground the tiles reach, while the figures count only what falls inside a US county. Other classes and unclassified ground are transparent. Below the zoom where individual fields are legible the county choropleth is shown instead.

yield.note: Yield forecast panel is reserved: the US yield model is in training and will be added without changing this layout.

weeks.area_basis_note: Direct count of the pixels the classifier labelled, at the native 5 m segmentation grid, deduplicated across overlapping MGRS tiles by deepest-inside ownership, then binned to 120 m cells for the county and state roll-up. Counted only inside US county geometry, so the belt, the states and the counties are the same cells and the parts sum to the whole; the class map layer draws the full classified extent, including the Canadian ground the tiles reach, which no figure here counts. County boundaries are the 1:500,000 generalised file, so roughly 6 k acres of genuine US crop within two cells of a border falls outside it and is lost -- 0.007% of the belt, and it under-counts rather than over-claims. This is the area OF the published map.

County and state boundaries: US Census Bureau cartographic boundary files (2022). Basemap © OpenStreetMap contributors; satellite imagery © Esri. method_html:
How the numbers are made

Every week, for each of the 280 HLS tiles covering the 12-state Corn Belt and its margins, the two-year HLS time series up to the forecast Monday is turned into trailing 30-day reflectance composites plus six prior years of CDL crop rotation, and a calibrated classifier predicts corn / soybean / other for every 30 m pixel.

That per-pixel classification is then refined against field boundaries. A Delineate-Anything segmentation of the same tiles, built from several cloud-free dates across the season, supplies the fields; each field takes the label its own pixels agree on, ground that has not grown corn or soybean in six years of CDL keeps its own label rather than being absorbed into the field, and the result is published at 5 m.

On the USDA comparison. June Acreage is a probability survey of farm operators, not a measurement. It is revised in later reports and the released figures carry no error term, so the benchmark here is drawn as though the survey were exact. A gap is a disagreement between two estimates. Where a difference is corroborated by the Cropland Data Layer as well, which is an independent classification, we treat it as real and say where it comes from.

What is counted. The headline is a direct pixel count of that published 5 m map -- not an adjusted or modelled total -- so the number and the picture are the same pixels. Crop labelled outside any delineated field, and isolated speckle, are treated as misclassification and are not counted: the quantity is the area of classified fields. Counting stops at the border. The tiles reach past it, so the map also draws classified fields in southern Ontario and the Canadian prairie; those are excluded from every figure here, which is why the counties add up to their state and the states to the belt. The 95% interval is classification error from the model's own error matrix at this lead time; it is not a sampling error and it does not cover the boundary between what counts as a field and what does not. Error-adjusted and survey-calibrated estimates are computed alongside and disclosed in the data, but they are not the published figure. Early in the season the model sees only emergence and the interval is wide; it narrows as canopies develop. The yield panel is reserved for the US yield model now in training.
